experiments.title: CompletableFuture Blocking the ForkJoinPool
experiments.subtitle: Why thenApply() with JDBC starves your entire async pipeline
experiments.scenario: A payment aggregation service chains 20 CompletableFuture steps to fan out balance lookups across 8 downstream ledgers and then merge the results. One step in the chain performs a synchronous JDBC call inside thenApply() to load supplemental account metadata. Under normal load this is invisible, but during month-end batch processing all ForkJoinPool worker threads block waiting on JDBC, completely starving all other CompletableFuture chains in the JVM—including unrelated real-time payment authorizations.
experiments.impact: During month-end reconciliation, the ForkJoinPool common pool (default size = CPU cores - 1) saturates within seconds. Real-time payment authorization latency spikes from 80ms to 45 seconds. Downstream services receive timeout errors. Card-not-present fraud checks are skipped by fallback logic, increasing fraud loss exposure by an estimated $200K per hour of degradation.

// jdbcRepo.findById() issues a blocking JDBC call

experiments.failureExplanation: CompletableFuture.thenApply() runs the function on whichever thread completed the previous stage — typically a ForkJoinPool worker. JDBC calls block that thread for the full network + query round-trip (5–30s under load). The ForkJoinPool common pool defaults to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1 threads, so on an 8-core host there are only 7 workers. When all 7 are blocked on JDBC, every new CompletableFuture task — across all chains in the JVM — queues behind them. The pool cannot spawn new threads to compensate because it is work-stealing, not unbounded. The result is a JVM-wide async starvation cascade.

Using Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() means each JDBC call runs on a lightweight virtual thread that parks (not blocks) the OS thread during socket I/O, enabling hundreds of concurrent JDBC calls with no platform thread exhaustion.

experiments.performanceNotes: The ForkJoinPool common pool size is Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1, which on a 4-vCPU container is just 3 threads. A single slow JDBC query (500ms) blocks a full 33% of pool capacity. Virtual threads eliminate this ceiling entirely: the JVM can run millions of parked virtual threads with minimal overhead, as the OS thread is reclaimed during I/O waits.

assessment.text: Why does thenApply() with a JDBC call cause ForkJoinPool starvation, but thenApplyAsync() with a dedicated executor does not?
options: A) thenApply() creates a new OS thread per call, overwhelming the OS scheduler

B) thenApply() runs the function on the FJP worker that completed the prior stage, blocking it during JDBC I/O, while thenApplyAsync() hands off to the supplied executor so the FJP worker is released immediately
C) JDBC drivers are incompatible with ForkJoinPool threads and throw exceptions
D) thenApply() uses a synchronized block internally that contends with the FJP work queue
assessment.explanation: thenApply() reuses the completing thread (a FJP worker) for the next stage. When that stage blocks on JDBC, the FJP worker is unavailable for other tasks. thenApplyAsync() with an executor enqueues the work there and returns the FJP worker to the pool immediately.

assessment.text: On a 4-vCPU container, what is the default ForkJoinPool common pool size, and what is the maximum number of simultaneous blocking thenApply() calls before all new CF tasks are queued?
options: A) 4 threads; 4 blocking calls exhaust the pool
B) 3 threads; 3 blocking calls exhaust the pool
C) Unbounded; FJP grows dynamically like a cached thread pool
D) 200 threads; matches Spring Boot default thread pool
assessment.explanation: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() defaults to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1 = 3 on a 4-vCPU host. After 3 concurrent blocking stages, the pool is fully saturated and all new tasks must wait in the queue.

assessment.text: Which Java 21 feature eliminates the need to explicitly size a blocking executor pool for JDBC workloads in CompletableFuture pipelines?
options: A) Record classes — they reduce object allocation pressure
B) Sealed interfaces — they enforce type-safe async results
C) Virtual threads via Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() — each task gets a lightweight VT that parks (not blocks) its carrier OS thread during I/O
D) Pattern matching for switch — it simplifies async error handling
assessment.explanation: Virtual threads (JEP 444) are scheduled by the JVM, not the OS. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O (including JDBC socket reads), the carrier OS thread is released and can run other virtual threads. This makes unlimited-concurrency JDBC pools safe without exhausting platform threads.

experiments.title: Virtual Thread Pinning via Synchronized Block
experiments.subtitle: How synchronized defeats the scalability promise of Java 21 virtual threads
experiments.scenario: A digital banking API is migrated from Spring Boot 3 (platform threads) to Spring Boot 4 with Java 21 virtual threads enabled globally via spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. The team expects to handle 100,000 concurrent requests on a 4-core host. After deployment, throughput is no better than the previous 200 platform-thread configuration. Profiling shows the getBalance() method — the hottest path, called on every API request — uses a synchronized method keyword acquired before a blocking JDBC query.
experiments.impact: Virtual thread adoption yields zero benefit on the getBalance() hot path. The service handles the same 200 req/s as before. During peak hours (09:00–10:00 market open), the carrier thread pool saturates and request latency degrades from 50ms to 8 seconds. The business loses an estimated $80K/hour in trading commissions on delayed order-book requests that depend on balance checks.

// for the ENTIRE duration of the JDBC call — defeating virtual thread I/O parking

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: synchronized on an instance method acquires the intrinsic monitor (object lock) of this BalanceService instance
UNSAFE: while holding the intrinsic monitor, the virtual thread blocks on JDBC I/O — the JVM cannot unmount it from the carrier thread because intrinsic locks are not yieldable
UNSAFE: carrier OS thread is pinned until queryForObject() returns — 100 concurrent VTs = 100 pinned carriers = same as platform threads

experiments.failureExplanation: Java 21 virtual threads achieve high concurrency by mounting/unmounting on carrier OS threads: when a VT blocks on I/O, it unmounts and the carrier is free to run another VT. However, the JVM cannot unmount a virtual thread that is holding a Java intrinsic monitor (synchronized block/method). The VT is 'pinned' — it occupies its carrier OS thread for the full duration of the lock, including the JDBC blocking I/O. With a default carrier pool of 4 (= vCPU count), only 4 concurrent synchronized calls can proceed; all others park waiting for a carrier. The throughput ceiling is identical to 4 platform threads.

simulation.safeAnnotation: ReentrantLock is implemented in Java (java.util.concurrent) and does not use intrinsic monitors. Virtual threads can unmount from their carrier while parked waiting on a ReentrantLock or during I/O within a lock, restoring full virtual-thread scalability.

correctCode: // ReentrantLock does NOT pin virtual threads — VTs can unmount
// from their carrier OS thread while waiting for or holding this lock
private final ReentrantLock balanceLock = new ReentrantLock();
// Always release in finally — prevents lock leak on exception
experiments.correctExplanation: ReentrantLock uses AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS) which parks threads via LockSupport.park() — a yieldable operation that allows virtual threads to unmount from their carrier OS thread. This means the carrier is free to run other virtual threads while VT-1 waits for I/O inside the lock, restoring the high-concurrency behavior promised by Java 21 virtual threads.

assessment.text: Why does the synchronized keyword on getBalance() prevent virtual threads from achieving high concurrency?
options: A) synchronized is deprecated in Java 21 and falls back to platform thread semantics
B) synchronized acquires an intrinsic monitor, which prevents the JVM from unmounting the virtual thread from its carrier OS thread during I/O, pinning the carrier for the full JDBC call duration
C) synchronized creates a new OS thread per invocation, overwhelming the scheduler
D) JDBC drivers detect synchronized and downgrade to synchronous mode
assessment.explanation: The JVM cannot unmount a virtual thread from its carrier while it holds an intrinsic monitor (synchronized). This pins the carrier OS thread for the full critical section duration, including any blocking I/O inside it. With 4 carriers, only 4 concurrent getBalance() calls can proceed — identical to 4 platform threads.

assessment.text: Which JVM diagnostic flag reveals virtual thread pinning events with full stack traces during testing?
options: A) -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=0
B) -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full
C) -XX:+PrintVirtualThreadStacks
D) -Dspring.threads.virtual.debug=true
assessment.explanation: -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full is a JVM diagnostic flag introduced in Java 21 that prints a stack trace to stdout whenever a virtual thread is pinned to its carrier thread, enabling you to identify pinning hotspots.

assessment.text: ReentrantLock allows virtual threads to unmount during I/O inside a lock. What is the key mechanism that makes this possible?
options: A) ReentrantLock uses native OS mutexes, which are non-blocking
B) ReentrantLock uses AbstractQueuedSynchronizer with LockSupport.park(), which is a yieldable operation — the JVM can unmount the VT from its carrier while parked
C) ReentrantLock automatically detects virtual threads and skips locking
D) ReentrantLock splits the JDBC call across multiple carrier threads
assessment.explanation: ReentrantLock is built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS), which uses LockSupport.park() to block waiting threads. park() is a yieldable operation recognized by the JVM scheduler, allowing virtual threads to unmount from their carrier and free it for other work — unlike intrinsic monitors which are not yieldable.

experiments.title: Missing Cancellation Leaks Resources on Timeout
experiments.subtitle: Why future.get(timeout) alone leaves orphaned connections, threads, and upstream calls
experiments.scenario: A payment authorization service must meet a 2-second SLA before declining a transaction. It calls an external fraud-scoring service via async HTTP and enforces the SLA with future.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS). After deployment, operations notices the HTTP connection pool to the fraud service slowly exhausts overnight. Investigation reveals that every timed-out authorization leaves an HTTP connection open for 30 seconds (the fraud service's read timeout), consuming a connection pool slot, a background thread, and 2MB of heap until the upstream call eventually completes.
experiments.impact: With 50 payment authorizations per second and a 5% fraud service latency spike rate, 2.5 orphaned connections are created per second. After 90 seconds the 200-connection pool exhausts. New authorizations fail with connection acquisition timeout errors. All payments are declined as a safety fallback, causing an estimated revenue loss of $450K per hour during outages. The issue is invisible in APM dashboards because the CompletableFuture completes with TimeoutException — no error is logged for the upstream leak.

// fraudCheckClient HTTP call continues running for 30s
// Connection pool slot held, background thread alive
throw new PaymentTimeoutException("Fraud check timeout", e);

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: future.get(2, SECONDS) only stops this thread from waiting — it does NOT cancel the CompletableFuture or its upstream HTTP call
UNSAFE: TimeoutException is caught but no cancellation is issued — the HTTP connection to fraud service stays open
UNSAFE: fraudCheckClient continues executing the HTTP call for up to 30 more seconds (read timeout), holding a connection pool slot
UNSAFE: background thread executing the future is also still running, consuming thread pool capacity

experiments.failureExplanation: CompletableFuture.get(timeout) is a blocking wait with a local timeout — it only stops the calling thread from waiting, but does not signal the CompletableFuture to stop executing. The upstream HTTP call that backs the future continues independently until its own I/O timeout fires (30s in this case). Every timed-out authorization leaves one HTTP connection open, one thread running, and memory allocated for the in-flight request. Because these orphans accumulate faster than they expire, the HTTP connection pool exhausts linearly until all new authorizations fail.

experiments.correctExplanation: future.cancel(true) completes the CompletableFuture with a CancellationException and sends an interrupt to the thread executing the future. If the HTTP client is interrupt-aware (java.net.http.HttpClient, OkHttp, Apache HttpClient 5), it closes the socket immediately, returning the connection to the pool. CompletableFuture.orTimeout() (Java 9+) is a declarative alternative that cancels the future automatically when the timeout fires, without requiring explicit try/catch management.

assessment.text: What is the fundamental problem with catching TimeoutException after future.get(2, SECONDS) without calling future.cancel(true)?
options: A) The future is automatically garbage collected and the HTTP connection is closed by the GC
B) future.get(timeout) only stops the calling thread from waiting — the CompletableFuture continues executing, keeping the HTTP connection open until the upstream call's own timeout fires
C) TimeoutException cancels the future automatically in Java 11+
D) The HTTP client closes the connection when the future completes with any exception
assessment.explanation: future.get(timeout) is a local wait with a timeout on the calling thread. It has no effect on the CompletableFuture itself — the future continues executing independently. Only future.cancel(true) signals the future to stop and interrupts the executing thread.

assessment.text: Which Java 9+ method provides declarative timeout-with-cancellation on a CompletableFuture, eliminating the need for manual cancel() calls?
options: A) future.completeOnTimeout(fallback, 2, SECONDS)
B) future.orTimeout(2, SECONDS)
C) future.exceptionally(e -> null)
D) future.thenApply(r -> r).get(2, SECONDS)
assessment.explanation: CompletableFuture.orTimeout(duration, unit) completes the future exceptionally with TimeoutException if it does not complete within the given duration, and also cancels downstream stages. It eliminates the need for manual try/catch/cancel patterns.

assessment.text: In Java 21 Structured Concurrency, which method guarantees that all forked subtasks are cancelled when the scope exits, including on timeout?
options: A) scope.fork(() -> ...).cancel()
B) The try-with-resources block — scope.close() cancels all running forks when the scope exits for any reason
C) StructuredTaskScope automatically sets a 2-second default timeout
D) scope.join() cancels remaining tasks after the first completes
assessment.explanation: StructuredTaskScope implements AutoCloseable. When the try-with-resources block exits — whether normally, via exception, or via joinUntil() deadline — scope.close() is called, which cancels all forks that have not yet completed. This provides a strong guarantee that no subtasks outlive the scope.

experiments.title: MDC Context Loss in Reactive Pipeline
experiments.subtitle: Why ThreadLocal tracing disappears after publishOn() and how to restore it
experiments.scenario: A payments microservice built on Spring WebFlux and Project Reactor assigns a correlation ID to each incoming HTTP request and stores it in MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context) for structured log correlation. The ID is visible in logs during the initial Mono assembly, but after publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) — used to offload a blocking fraud check — the traceId key disappears from all subsequent log statements. Production incidents on the payment processing path cannot be traced end-to-end because distributed traces lose their correlation ID across thread boundaries.
experiments.impact: On average, 40% of payment processing log events have no traceId after the publishOn() switch. During a fraud service latency event affecting 15,000 transactions per hour, the ops team cannot correlate payment authorization failures with specific customer accounts. MTTR (mean time to resolve) increases from 12 minutes to 4 hours. Per SLA, delayed resolution incurs $5,000/hour in contractual penalties plus reputational risk from customer complaints.
incorrectCode: public Mono<PaymentResult> process(Payment payment, String traceId) {
// MDC set on the HTTP thread — visible here
// Thread switch: Reactor assigns a boundedElastic thread

assessment.text: Why does MDC.put('traceId', id) on the HTTP thread not appear in log events emitted after publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())?
options: A) publishOn() clears all MDC values as a security measure to prevent context leakage
B) MDC is backed by ThreadLocal — values are per-thread and not copied when Reactor switches execution to a different scheduler thread via publishOn()
C) boundedElastic() creates a new ClassLoader, making the MDC class incompatible
D) Reactor automatically uses Reactor context for MDC, overriding the ThreadLocal values
assessment.explanation: SLF4J MDC uses a ThreadLocal<Map> under the hood. Each OS thread has its own independent MDC map. publishOn() changes which thread executes downstream operators. The new scheduler thread has never had MDC.put() called on it, so its MDC map is empty.

assessment.text: What is the purpose of calling doFinally(signal -> MDC.remove('traceId')) in the correct implementation?
options: A) It improves performance by freeing the ThreadLocal memory faster
B) It prevents the traceId from being included in error log events
C) boundedElastic threads are reused across requests — without cleanup, a previous request's traceId remains in MDC and contaminates log events for subsequent requests processed on the same thread
D) It signals Reactor context to remove the traceId from the subscription context
assessment.explanation: Scheduler threads are pooled and reused. If MDC.remove() is not called after the pipeline completes, the traceId set for request A remains in that thread's MDC map. When the same thread is reused for request B, request B's log events will incorrectly include request A's traceId — a silent context leak that is very hard to debug.

assessment.text: Which Reactor operator is used to read values from the subscription's Reactor context and make them available as Java objects at subscription time?
options: A) Mono.fromCallable(() -> ReactorContext.get('traceId'))
B) Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> Mono.just(ctx.get('traceId')))
C) Mono.just(payment).contextRead(ctx -> ctx.get('traceId'))
D) Flux.fromContext().filter(ctx -> ctx.hasKey('traceId'))
assessment.explanation: Mono.deferContextual(contextView -> ...) defers the creation of the Mono until subscription time and provides the ContextView as an argument. This is the idiomatic way to read values from Reactor context and bridge them to ThreadLocal APIs like MDC.

experiments.title: Backpressure Violation in Payment Event Stream
experiments.subtitle: Silent event drops when producer outpaces consumer in a Flux pipeline
experiments.scenario: A real-time payment event processor consumes a Kafka topic publishing settlement events at 50,000 events per second during end-of-day batch settlement. The events are wrapped in a Flux using Flux.create() with the default buffer overflow strategy. A downstream enrichment step — which calls a database to add account metadata — processes at 500 events per second. The in-memory buffer fills silently, and beyond the default 256-event buffer, events are dropped with no error, no log message, and no metric. Settlement payments go unprocessed without any alert.
experiments.impact: During a 10-minute end-of-day settlement window, the system drops approximately 29.7 million events (50,000 - 500 events/sec * 600 seconds). Each dropped event represents a payment settlement that never completes. Affected customers see balance discrepancies until the next reconciliation cycle (24 hours). Regulatory reporting is incorrect. The firm faces potential Central Bank fines of up to €500K per incident for incomplete settlement records.
incorrectCode: // UNSAFE: Kafka consumer pushes at 50,000 events/sec
// flatMap requests Integer.MAX_VALUE concurrency by default
// — no backpressure signaled to Kafka consumer

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: Flux.create() with default OverflowStrategy.BUFFER silently buffers up to 256 events then drops all further events with no error
UNSAFE: kafkaConsumer.subscribe() pushes events as fast as Kafka delivers them — there is no mechanism for the subscriber to signal 'slow down'
UNSAFE: flatMap with default concurrency (Integer.MAX_VALUE) does not propagate backpressure upstream — it absorbs all events into unbounded inner subscriptions
UNSAFE: the error handler never fires for dropped events — OverflowStrategy.BUFFER drop is completely silent

experiments.failureExplanation: Reactive Streams backpressure requires the subscriber to request a specific number of items from the publisher. Flux.create() with OverflowStrategy.BUFFER creates a push-based source that ignores downstream request signals — it accepts items as fast as the producer provides them and buffers up to 256 (the default queue size). When the buffer is full and the downstream is still processing, additional items are silently dropped. flatMap() compounds the problem by default: it requests Integer.MAX_VALUE items upstream, effectively disabling request-based backpressure. The result is data loss with no observable signal.

The onBackpressureDrop with an explicit metric and log provides a last-resort safety net that is observable, never silent.

assessment.text: What happens by default when a Flux.create() source produces events faster than the downstream subscriber can consume them?
options: A) The publisher automatically slows down to match the subscriber's processing rate
B) An exception is thrown immediately and the stream terminates with an error
C) Events are buffered up to 256 items (default queue size) and silently dropped beyond that — no exception, no log, no metric
D) The flatMap operator queues all events in a LinkedList until the subscriber catches up
assessment.explanation: Flux.create() defaults to OverflowStrategy.BUFFER with a queue of 256 items. When the queue fills, additional items from the source are silently discarded. No onError is fired, no log is emitted, and the subscriber never knows events were lost.

assessment.text: What does the limitRate(n) operator do in a Reactor pipeline, and why does it help with backpressure?
options: A) It limits the total number of elements the Flux will emit over its lifetime
B) It issues a request(n) signal upstream and replenishes when 75% of the batch is consumed, aligning the upstream delivery rate with the downstream processing capacity
C) It throttles the subscriber to process at most n events per second
D) It limits the number of concurrent flatMap inner subscriptions to n
assessment.explanation: limitRate(n) implements demand-based flow control: it requests n items from upstream, and when 75% have been processed downstream, it requests another batch. This ensures the upstream producer never delivers more items than the downstream can handle, preventing buffer overflow.

assessment.text: Which Flux.create() OverflowStrategy is most appropriate for a payment settlement stream where event loss is unacceptable?
options: A) OverflowStrategy.LATEST — keep only the most recent payment event
B) OverflowStrategy.DROP — discard the oldest events to make room for new ones
C) OverflowStrategy.ERROR — immediately fail the stream with an overflow exception, triggering the error handler and preventing silent data loss
D) OverflowStrategy.IGNORE — bypass backpressure entirely for maximum throughput
assessment.explanation: OverflowStrategy.ERROR causes the stream to signal onError immediately when the buffer is full. This prevents silent data loss by forcing the system to fail fast — the error handler fires, alerts are triggered, and the team is notified. For settlement data, a visible failure is always preferable to silent data loss.

experiments.title: Structured Concurrency Partial Failure Not Propagated
experiments.subtitle: Why StructuredTaskScope.join() without ShutdownOnFailure approves partial payment authorizations
experiments.scenario: A payment authorization service uses Java 21 Structured Concurrency to run three compliance checks in parallel: fraud scoring, KYC (Know Your Customer) verification, and credit limit validation. The team uses a plain StructuredTaskScope to fork all three tasks and joins them before assembling the authorization result. During testing, the KYC service throws a ServiceUnavailableException. The scope.join() returns normally. The code then calls kyc.get() which throws, but the caller catches it as a generic exception and logs it — the payment is approved based on only fraud and limit checks. A KYC-failing customer receives authorization.
experiments.impact: During a 4-hour KYC service outage, 2,340 payment authorizations are approved without KYC verification. Post-incident analysis reveals 18 of those customers are on watchlists. The firm faces regulatory enforcement action under AML (Anti-Money Laundering) regulations, with potential fines of €1M–€10M and mandatory external audit. The incident is classified as a Tier-1 compliance failure.
incorrectCode: public AuthResult authorize(Payment payment) throws Exception {
// UNSAFE: plain StructuredTaskScope does NOT enforce failure policy
// UNSAFE: join() waits for ALL subtasks but does NOT propagate failures
// If kyc throws, scope still returns normally here
// UNSAFE: fraud.get() / kyc.get() / limit.get() may throw ExecutionException
// If the caller silently swallows it, partial auth proceeds

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: StructuredTaskScope<Object> has no built-in failure policy — it is a base class intended for custom policies only
UNSAFE: scope.join() returns normally even if one or more subtasks threw an exception — it only waits for all tasks to complete (success or failure)
UNSAFE: fraud.get() / kyc.get() / limit.get() throw ExecutionException if the subtask failed — but the caller may catch or ignore this, assembling a partial AuthResult
UNSAFE: if kycService threw ServiceUnavailableException, kyc.get() throws — but code may still reach limitService.check() result, partial auth assembled

experiments.failureExplanation: StructuredTaskScope.join() waits for all forked tasks to either complete successfully or fail, but it does not inspect or propagate individual task failures. After join() returns, each subtask's outcome must be checked manually via Subtask.get() or Subtask.state(). If the caller calls subtask.get() on a failed task, an ExecutionException is thrown — but if this exception is caught somewhere up the call stack and the code continues assembling the AuthResult with the available results, a partial authorization is constructed. The fundamental issue is that plain StructuredTaskScope provides no failure policy enforcement.

correctCode: public AuthResult authorize(Payment payment) throws Exception {
// SAFE: ShutdownOnFailure cancels all subtasks if any one fails
// join() waits for all tasks OR for the first failure to trigger shutdown
// SAFE: throwIfFailed() re-throws the first subtask exception
// If any check failed, this throws — AuthResult is never assembled
// Only reachable if ALL three checks succeeded
experiments.correctExplanation: StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure is a built-in policy scope that calls scope.shutdown() as soon as any forked subtask fails. After scope.join() returns, scope.throwIfFailed() re-throws the exception from the first failed subtask, guaranteeing the caller receives the failure before any result assembly code is reached. The pattern is fail-fast: either all three checks succeed and AuthResult is assembled, or the first failure throws and payment is declined.

assessment.text: What is the fundamental difference between StructuredTaskScope and StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure?
options: A) StructuredTaskScope runs tasks sequentially; ShutdownOnFailure runs them in parallel

B) StructuredTaskScope has no built-in failure policy — join() returns normally even if subtasks failed; ShutdownOnFailure cancels remaining subtasks on the first failure and throwIfFailed() re-throws it after join()
C) ShutdownOnFailure retries failed subtasks automatically before propagating the exception
D) StructuredTaskScope uses the ForkJoinPool; ShutdownOnFailure uses virtual threads
assessment.explanation: StructuredTaskScope is the base class with no policy — it simply waits for all tasks and lets the developer inspect results manually. ShutdownOnFailure is a built-in subclass that implements the fail-fast policy: on the first subtask failure it cancels remaining tasks, and throwIfFailed() ensures the failure is re-thrown after join(), preventing partial result assembly.

assessment.text: In the buggy implementation, why might a payment be approved even though kycService.check() threw an exception?
options: A) scope.join() catches and suppresses all subtask exceptions
B) KYC failures are automatically retried by the JVM structured concurrency framework

C) After scope.join() returns normally, calling kyc.get() throws ExecutionException, but if that exception is caught by a generic catch block somewhere in the call stack, execution continues and AuthResult may be assembled from fraud.get() and limit.get() alone
D) StructuredTaskScope guarantees at-least-two-out-of-three success for authorization
assessment.explanation: scope.join() returns normally regardless of subtask outcomes. kyc.get() throws ExecutionException for a failed subtask. If the caller or any layer in the call stack catches this with a generic Exception handler and continues, the code proceeds to construct AuthResult. With fraud.get() and limit.get() both succeeding, a partial (and compliance-violating) AuthResult is returned.

assessment.text: Which line must immediately follow scope.join() to guarantee no partial result is assembled after any subtask failure?
options: A) if (fraud.state() == FAILED || kyc.state() == FAILED || limit.state() == FAILED) return null;
B) scope.throwIfFailed(); — re-throws the first subtask exception, preventing any subsequent code from executing if a failure occurred
C) scope.close(); — closes the scope and propagates failures
D) scope.shutdown(); — explicitly shuts down any remaining tasks
assessment.explanation: scope.throwIfFailed() (available on ShutdownOnFailure) checks if any subtask failed and re-throws the exception. Because it throws, the subsequent AuthResult construction code is unreachable if any subtask failed. Option A is brittle manual state checking that is easy to get wrong. scope.close() and scope.shutdown() do not re-throw subtask exceptions.
